questions.prompt: At a point where \(f\) is differentiable, a vector \(d\) is a descent direction when
options: \(d\) is a multiple of the all-ones vector
questions.explanation: The directional derivative is the dot product \(\nabla f(x)^T d\). A strict negative value means the first-order model decreases along \(d\), which is the definition of a descent direction. A zero dot product is a tangent direction of the model, and a positive dot product is an ascent direction. Being a multiple of the all-ones vector says nothing about \(f\).

questions.prompt: Let \(\nabla f(x) = (3, 1)\) and \(d = (-2, 1)\). What is the directional derivative \(\nabla f(x)^T d\)?
questions.explanation: The dot product is \(3 \cdot (-2) + 1 \cdot 1 = -6 + 1 = -5\). The value is negative, so \(d\) is a descent direction, but the question asks for the derivative itself. Reporting \(5\) drops the sign. Reporting \(-6\) stops after the first term. Reporting \(1\) is the second component of \(d\).

questions.prompt: If \(\nabla f(x)^T d < 0\), the first-order expansion implies that
options: \(f(x + t d) < f(x)\) for all sufficiently small \(t > 0\)
the Hessian at \(x\) is positive definite
questions.explanation: Write \(f(x + t d) = f(x) + t\, \nabla f(x)^T d + o(t)\). The linear term is negative and dominates the remainder when \(t > 0\) is small enough, so the function drops. A long step can turn back up, so the decrease is not guaranteed for every positive \(t\). A negative directional derivative means \(x\) is not a local minimizer. The Hessian is not involved in this first-order argument.
questions.figure_alt: A straight line sloping downward on labeled axes.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the order that proves a negative directional derivative produces a decrease for a short step. Each step uses the result of the step before it.
questions.explanation: The expansion has to be written before it can be divided by the step. The divided form is what the little-o term no longer hides, so the sign of the directional derivative can be read off only after that division. The function decrease is the difference quotient multiplied back by the positive step, which preserves the inequality. Multiplying before the sign is known does not yet prove a decrease.

questions.figure_alt: A solid segment joins two marked points on a dashed line.
steps: Expand \(f(x + t d) = f(x) + t\, \nabla f(x)^T d + o(t)\) as \(t \to 0\).
Divide the change in \(f\) by \(t > 0\), leaving \(\nabla f(x)^T d + o(1)\).
For small \(t > 0\) the negative directional derivative dominates, so the difference quotient is negative.
Multiply that negative quotient by \(t > 0\) to conclude \(f(x + t d) < f(x)\).

questions.prompt: Let \(\nabla f(x) = (1, -2)\). Which of these vectors are descent directions at \(x\)?
questions.explanation:
A descent direction needs a strictly negative dot product with \((1, -2)\).
• \((-1, 0)\) gives \(-1\).
• \((1, 1)\) gives \(1 - 2 = -1\).
• \((-3, -1)\) gives \(-3 + 2 = -1\).
• \((2, 1)\) gives \(2 - 2 = 0\), which is not strict.
• \((4, 1)\) gives \(4 - 2 = 2\), an ascent direction.

questions.prompt: The gradient is \((p, q)\) and the direction is \((-p, r)\). The directional derivative equals
questions.explanation: The dot product is \(p \cdot (-p) + q \cdot r = -p^2 + q r\). Every declared name appears: \(p\) from the first components, and \(q\) and \(r\) from the second. Dropping the minus sign turns the square into an ascent contribution. Using \(p \cdot r\) instead of \(q \cdot r\) pairs the wrong components. Replacing \(r\) by \(-p\) computes the steepest-descent derivative \(-p^2 - q^2\), which is a different direction.

questions.prompt: A note checks \(d = (1, -1)\) for \(f(x_1, x_2) = x_1^2 + 2 x_2\) at \((1, 0)\). Exactly one step is a false claim.
questions.explanation: The partial derivatives of \(x_1^2 + 2 x_2\) are \((2 x_1, 2)\), and at \((1, 0)\) that is \((2, 2)\). The dot product with \((1, -1)\) is \(2 - 2 = 0\). The negative gradient \((-2, -2)\) dots with \((2, 2)\) to give \(-8 < 0\), so that direction does descend. The false step is the reading of the zero: a descent direction requires a strictly negative directional derivative. Zero means the first-order model is flat along \(d\).
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 280 180" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>a segment</title><line x1="28" y1="150" x2="256" y2="150"/><polygon points="256,150 249.6,152.7 249.6,147.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><line x1="40" y1="164" x2="40" y2="20"/><polygon points="40,20 42.7,26.4 37.3,26.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="250" y="166" text-anchor="end" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x1</text><text x="48" y="16" text-anchor="start" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x2</text><line x1="36" y1="132" x2="244" y2="36" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/><line x1="70" y1="112" x2="190" y2="52" stroke-width="2.4"/><circle cx="70" cy="112" r="2.6" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="190" cy="52" r="2.6" fill="currentColor"/></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A solid segment joins two marked points on a dashed line.
steps: The gradient is \((2 x_1, 2)\), so it equals \((2, 2)\) at \((1, 0)\).
A directional derivative of zero means \(d\) is a descent direction.
The direction \(-\nabla f = (-2, -2)\) has directional derivative \(-8\), so it is a descent direction.
reasons: A zero directional derivative is not the strict inequality that defines a descent direction.
The dot product \(2 - 2\) is not zero.

First \(D

questions.prompt:
If \(D\) is symmetric positive definite and \(
abla f(x) 
e 0\), the vector \(d = -D 
abla f(x)\) is a descent direction because
options: every positive definite matrix has negative eigenvalues
questions.explanation:
Substitute the direction: the directional derivative equals \(-
abla f^T D 
abla f\). Positive definiteness makes that quadratic form positive whenever the gradient is nonzero, so the directional derivative is negative. A positive definite matrix has positive eigenvalues and a nonzero determinant. The direction \(-D 
abla f\) is orthogonal to the gradient only in special cases, not in general.

questions.prompt: Once a descent direction has been chosen, the next decision in a descent iteration is
options: to discard the direction and use a simplex basis instead
to replace the gradient by the Hessian and stop
to choose a step length along that direction
to set the gradient to zero by hand
questions.explanation: A descent direction says which way a short move decreases the first-order model. The iteration still has to choose how far to go. That choice is the step length. Setting the gradient to zero is the optimality condition at a minimizer, not the next algorithmic step. A simplex basis is a construction for a linear program. The Hessian may be used later to build a different direction, and it does not replace the step-length decision.

questions.prompt: Let \(\nabla f(x) = (6, 1)\) and \(d = (-1, 2)\). What is \(\nabla f(x)^T d\)?
questions.explanation: The dot product is \(6 \cdot (-1) + 1 \cdot 2 = -6 + 2 = -4\). The negative value says \(d\) is a descent direction. Reporting \(4\) drops the sign. Reporting \(-6\) ignores the second term. Reporting \(8\) is the product of the two second components with the wrong sign pattern, \(1 \cdot 2\) added to \(6\) instead of subtracted.

questions.prompt: A line-search rule such as a sufficient-decrease test is applied
options: to a direction that has already been chosen
only when the Hessian is indefinite
in place of checking that the directional derivative is negative
questions.explanation: The sufficient-decrease test compares function values along a ray \(x + t d\). That ray exists only after \(d\) has been chosen. The gradient is an input to the direction, so it is computed first. An indefinite Hessian can still leave a descent direction available, and the line search does not wait for that case. The line search does not replace the sign check: the sign check is what makes a small enough step able to pass.
questions.figure_alt: A straight line sloping downward on labeled axes.
